title: The Anyon Atlas
authors: Jonah Berean-Dutcher, Clay Cordova, Julio Parra-Martinez, Richard Tuddenham
abstract: We classify possible topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions with up to 22 anyons in the bosonic case and up to 26 in the fermionic case, through the modular data of modular and supermodular tensor categories. We construct such data via congruence representations of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ using a numerical optimization algorithm that scales to high rank. We chart the relations between the resulting theories, including anyon condensations and Chern-Simons realizations. We find examples of modular data that do not appear to arise from any Chern-Simons theory by any sequence of condensations of anyons or gaugings of ordinary global symmetries. These examples give qualitatively new topological quantum field theories, which go beyond any notion of gauge theory. For examples in this class with 11 and 12 anyon types, we solve the pentagon and hexagon equations explicitly, showing that these modular data are realized by full unitary topological quantum field theories. We also introduce https://www.AnyonAtlas.org, an online resource for exploring the data.
summary: This paper classifies topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions by analyzing their underlying mathematical structure, the modular tensor category. The authors develop a computational method to catalog these theories, finding numerous examples that cannot be derived from conventional Chern-Simons gauge theories. This expands our understanding of topological order beyond established gauge theory paradigms.
main_problem: The goal is to classify all possible Topological Quantum Field Theories (TQFTs) in 2+1 dimensions and map the relationships between them, creating a comprehensive 'Anyon Atlas.'
main_result: The authors classify up to 22 bosonic and 26 fermionic TQFTs using modular/supermodular tensor categories, identifying examples that fundamentally go beyond descriptions based on Chern-Simons gauge theories.
method: Classification relies on analyzing the modular data (S, T) which defines a congruence representation of SL(2, Z), using a numerical optimization algorithm scaled to high ranks.
model_or_system: The theory concerns TQFTs describing anyons (quasiparticles with non-standard statistics) in 2+1 dimensions, mathematically characterized by unitary modular or supermodular tensor categories.
key_observables: Modular data (S, T), anyon types (up to 22 bosonic/26 fermionic), and satisfaction of the pentagon and hexagon equations.
important_parameters: The rank of the modular/supermodular category (up to 22 or 26).
main_assumptions: The classification is computationally intensive, and the authors admit that the current method does not provide an exact certificate that *every* possible set of modular data has been found.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the counts of identified modular and supermodular data at various ranks, categorized by pseudo-unitary, prime, and anisotropic types.
paper_structure: The paper systematically classifies modular data using numerical methods, analyzes the relationship between these data and Chern-Simons theories, and presents the findings in the online Anyon Atlas.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep mathematical framework for classifying exotic topological phases of matter, which is crucial for understanding fractional quantum Hall states and topological quantum computation beyond standard gauge theory models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Number of modular and supermodular data at each rank, with the total shown above the bars. The light bars count, respectively, all data and the subset which is pseudo-unitary, meaning that its quantum dimensions are positive and hence it could possibly correspond to a full unitary modular tensor category. The dark inner bars count the subset of the data which are prime, i.e. do not split into a product of lower-rank examples. Finally, the green bars count completely anisotropic data corresponding to terminal elements in a Witt class that do not admit any possible anyon condensation.

Figure 2: The Witt group is composed of equivalence classes of modular categories related by conden- sation and gauging, or, equivalently, 1- and 0-form gauging. Condensation between two phases, and its effect on simple lines, is illustrated schematically on the left. Two phases related by condensation admit a gapped domain wall interface. Anyonic excitations in one phase may be deconfined, surviving as freely propagating excitations in the condensed phase; confined, unable to propagate into the con- densed phase but surviving as excitations localized to the interface; or condensed, becoming identified with the vacuum in the condensed phase.
